questions.prompt: Why does `Dispose()` exist if .NET has a garbage collector?
options: The GC never runs unless `Dispose()` is called
`Dispose()` frees managed objects faster than the GC
Unmanaged resources such as file handles and DB connections are not cleaned up automatically, so `Dispose()` frees them explicitly
`Dispose()` is required on every class so it can be garbage collected
questions.explanation: The GC cleans up managed objects automatically, but unmanaged resources like OS file handles, native memory or DB connections are not; `Dispose()` lets you free them explicitly instead of waiting for finalization.

questions.prompt: An exception is thrown inside `using (var reader = new StreamReader("data.txt")) { ... }`. Is `reader` disposed?
options: No; `Dispose()` runs only when the block finishes normally
Yes; the `using` statement disposes the object when the block ends, even if an exception occurs
Only if you also call `reader.Dispose()` in a `catch` block
No; the object is disposed later by the garbage collector
questions.explanation: The `using` statement ensures the `IDisposable` object is disposed automatically when the block ends, even if an exception occurs. It is a cleaner alternative to calling `Dispose()` in try/finally.

questions.prompt: With a using declaration (C# 8+) such as `using StreamReader reader = File.OpenText("data.txt");`, when is `reader` disposed?
options: Immediately after the line runs
Only when the program exits
Never; declarations need an explicit `Dispose()` call
Automatically at the end of the enclosing method scope
questions.explanation: A using declaration has no braces; the object is disposed automatically at the end of the method scope.

questions.prompt: You can't use `using` for an `IDisposable` object. What does the note recommend instead?
options: Wrap the work in `try`/`finally` and call `.Dispose()` in the `finally` block
Call `.Dispose()` at the end of the `try` block
Call `GC.Collect()` after you are done
Set the variable to `null` so the resource is released
questions.explanation: If you skip `using`, wrap the object in a `try`/`finally` block and call `.Dispose()` in `finally` to guarantee cleanup even if exceptions occur.

questions.prompt: What does a `global using` directive do?
options: It disposes every object in the project automatically
It imports static members of a type
It applies the namespace import to all files in the project
It creates an alias for a long type name
questions.explanation: `global using` applies to all files in the project, which the note recommends in .NET 6+ projects to reduce boilerplate.
